Employee benefit obligations
A:	 Defined Contribution Plan
	
Superannuation Fund
	
The Corporation has Superannuation - Defined Contribution Scheme (DCS) maintained by ‘Superannuation Benefit Fund 
Scheme (SBFS) Trust’ wherein Employer makes a monthly contribution of a certain percentage of ‘Basic Salary & Dearness 
Allowance(DA)’, out of 30%, earmarked for various Superannuation benefits. This is in accordance with Department of Public 
Enterprises (DPE) guidelines. These contributions are credited to individual Employee’s Account maintained either with Life 
Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) or an optional National Pension Scheme (NPS) Account. For the Financial Year 2025-26, 
the Corporation has made an overall contribution of ₹ 214.75 Crore (2024-25: ₹ 190.56 Crore) towards Superannuation - DCS 
[including ₹ 146.81 Crore (2024-25: ₹ 105.78 Crore) to NPS] by charging it to the Statement of Profit and Loss.
	
Employee Pension Scheme(EPS-95)
	
During the year, Corporation has recognised ₹ 6.54 Crore (2024-25: ₹ 6.67 Crore) as contribution to Employee Pension Scheme 
(EPS-95) in the Statement of Profit and Loss.
B:	 Defined Benefit Plan
	
Provident Fund
	
Provident Fund is administered through a separate Trust, established for this purpose in accordance with The Employee 
Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. The Corporation’s contribution to the Provident Fund is remitted to 
this trust based on a fixed percentage of the eligible employee’s salary and charged to Statement of Profit and Loss. During 
the year, the Corporation has recognized ₹ 172.38 Crore (2024-25: ₹ 168.94 Crore) as Employer’s contribution to Provident Fund 
in the Statement of Profit and Loss.
	
Shortfall, if any, in matching the Government specified minimum rate of return, will be made good by the Corporation and 
charged to Statement of Profit and Loss. During the year, the fund has been able to match the Government specified minimum 
rate of return. The present value of benefit obligation at period end is ₹ 5,395.72 Crore (31.03.2025: ₹ 5,484.75 Crore). The fair 
value of the plan assets of Provident Fund Trust at the period end is ₹ 5,301.24 Crore (31.03.2025: ₹ 5,421.71 Crore) resulting 
in cumulative shortfall of ₹ 94.48 Crore (31.03.2025:₹ 63.04 Crore). For the current year, a shortfall of ₹ 22.10 Crore (2024-25: 
₹ 31.94 Crore) has been accounted through Other Comprehensive Income, and the balance has been charged to the Statement 
of Profit and Loss, as applicable.
	
During the current year, a provision of ₹ Nil Crore has been created/reversed [FY 2024-25: an amount ₹ 0.66 Crore was reversed] 
towards losses/reduction in losses on defaulted investments. The initial provision was created in FY 2019-20.

Pursuant to paragraph 57 of Ind AS 19, accounting by an entity for defined benefit plans, inter-alia, involves determining the 
amount of the net defined benefit liability (asset) which shall be adjusted for any effect of limiting a net defined benefit 
asset to the asset ceiling prescribed in paragraph 64. As per Para 64 of Ind AS 19, in case of surplus in a defined benefit 
plan, an entity shall measure the net defined benefit asset at the lower of actual surplus or the value of the assets ceiling 
determined using the discount rate. The asset ceiling is the present value of any economic benefits available in the form of 
refunds from the plan or reductions in future contributions to the plan. Further, paragraph 65 provides that a net defined 
benefit asset may arise where a defined benefit plan has been overfunded or where actuarial gains have arisen.
	
As per the provisions of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Company has no right 
to the benefits either in the form of refund from the plan or lower future contribution to the plan towards the net surplus 
of ₹ 4.49 Crore (31.03.2025: ₹ 16.99 Crore) determined through actuarial valuation. Accordingly, Company has not recognised 
the surplus as an asset, as these pertain to the Provident Fund Trust and not to the Company.

I.	
Gratuity: i) Each employee rendering continuous service of 5 Years or more is entitled to receive gratuity amount equal 
to 15/26 of the eligible salary for every completed years of service subject to maximum of ₹ 0.20 Crore at the time of 
separation from the Corporation. Besides the ceiling, gratuity increases by 25% whenever IDA rises by 50%. The long 
term employee benefit of Gratuity is administered through a Trust, established under the erstwhile Payment of Gratuity 
Act, 1972. The Board of Trustees comprises of representatives from the Employer who are also plan participants in 
accordance with the plans regulation. The liability towards gratuity is funded with Life Insurance Companies.
	
	
ii)	
Pursuant to notification of Code on Social Security during the year, Actuarial Valuation of (unfunded) Gratuity 
liability has been carried-out towards fixed-term associates with the Corporation as of 31.03.2026.
	
II.	
Pension: The employees covered by the Pension Plan of the Corporation are entitled to receive monthly pension for 
life. However, none of the current serving employees are covered under Pension Plan of the Corporation.
	
III.	 Post Retirement Medical Benefit (PRMBS): Post Retirement Benefit medical scheme provides medical benefit to 
retired employees and eligible dependent family members. This long term employee benefit is administered through a 
Trust. The liability towards Post-Retirement Medical Benefit for employees is ascertained, yearly, based on the actuarial 
valuation and funded to the Trust.
	
IV.	 Ex-gratia: The ex-employees of Corporation are covered under the Scheme, entitling to get ex-gratia, determined based 
on their salary grade at the time of their superannuation. The benefit is paid to eligible employees till their survival, and 
thereafter till the survival of their spouse. However, none of the current serving employees are covered under this Plan.
	
V.	
Resettlement Allowance: Upon superannuation from the services of the Corporation, there are employees who 
permanently settle down at a place other than the location of the last posting. Such employees are provided with 
resettlement allowance as per policy of the Corporation.
	
VI.	 Felicitation Scheme: Under the Scheme superannuated employees are felicitated with a token lumpsum amount to 
honor their long and dedicated service, on reaching certain age-related milestones.
	
VI.	 Others: The expected return on plan assets is based on market expectation over the entire life of the related obligation. 
The actuarial assumption with regard to future salary escalation takes into consideration, the factors such as inflation, 
seniority, promotion, demand & supply in the employment market.
	
VII.	 Figures in italics represent last year figures.
I:	
The Government of India has notified the implementation of four Labour Codes, namely The Code on Wages, 2019, The 
Industrial Relations Code, 2020, The Code on Social Security, 2020 and The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions 
Code, 2020, with effect from 21st November 2025. These Codes consolidate and rationalise 29 existing labour laws.
	
Based on the assessment carried out by the Corporation and the information available as at the reporting date, no material 
impact is envisaged in this regard. The Corporation continues to monitor developments on labour code/rules and provide 
appropriate accounting effect, as applicable.

The vision of a Sashakt Bharat is being redefined. As geopolitical shifts, 
supply chain disruptions, technological breakthroughs and evolving energy 
dynamics continue to reshape the global landscape, national strength can 
no longer be mea

sured solely by economic growth or resource availability. 
It is increasingly shaped by resilience, adaptability and the capability  to 
anticipate change. As India advances towards its long-term development 
ambitions, the need is not merely to build a stronger nation, but to reimagine 
what strength itself means in an era of unprecedented transformation.
For India, this reimagined vision lies in building resilient infrastructure, 
securing critical resources, fostering innovation, accelerating industrial 
capabilities and building institutions that can thrive amid uncertainty. 
The aim is  enhancing self-reliance while remaining globally connected, 
expanding opportunities while safeguarding stability, and shaping the 
foundations necessary to support the aspirations of a rapidly growing 
economy and society.
Reimagining 
Sashakt 
Against this backdrop, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) 
continues to play a pivotal role in enabling national progress. As the energy 
landscape undergoes significant change, the Company is strengthening 
its core business, expanding its capabilities and pursuing new avenues of 
growth to enhance long-term competitiveness. Through investments in 
capacity, diversification, technology and operational excellence, HPCL is 
preparing itself to address emerging opportunities while contributing to 
India’s evolving development priorities.
The theme, “Reimagining Sashakt Bharat” reflects this broader 
vision of nation-building. It embodies a commitment to looking beyond 
conventional definitions of growth and embracing new possibilities that 
strengthen economic resilience, energy preparedness and future readiness. 
As India embarks on its next phase of development,, HPCL remains focused 
on supporting a nation that is not only stronger today, but better equipped 
for the opportunities and complexities of the future.

Delivering Strong Performance
HPCL reported a record Profit After Tax of ₹17,175 crore. Revenue 
from Operations stood at ₹4,78,543 crore, while EBITDA reached 
₹33,182 crore. The Corporation achieved its highest-ever sales 
volume of 51.45 MMT, each figure is the sum of countless 
decisions taken well, seamless operations conducted on ground 
and the priceless trust our customers place in us every single 
day.
Project Samriddhi (the EBITDA improvement program of the 
corporation) delivered benefits of ₹ 1,691 crore through focused 
interventions in cost optimisation, operational excellence and 
margin enhancement.
We improved our balance sheet strength significantly during the 
year, supported by prudent capital allocation, disciplined cost 
management and a continued focus on operational excellence. 
Net worth stood at ₹59,847 crore as on March 31, 2026, while 
the debt-equity ratio improved to 0.80 from 1.38 as on March 
31, 2025. These achievements underscore our ability to navigate 
market volatility while remaining focused on long-term value 
creation. The improved balance sheet strength provided us the 
muscle to fight the challenges posed by West Asia crisis.
Refining Excellence
Refining continues to be one of HPCL’s strongest pillars of value 
creation. During FY 2025–26, our refineries processed a record 
crude throughput of 26.04 MMT. Capacity utilisation stood at 
106.3%, reflecting sustained operat

ional excellence and efficient 
asset management. Gross Refining Margin for the year stood at 
US$ 8.79 per barrel.
Visakh Refinery clocked its highest-ever annual crude throughput 
of 16.04 MMT (107% capacity utilisation), supported by improved 
reliability and effective use of upgraded process units.
A defining milestone of the year was the commissioning of 
the Residue Upgradation Facility (RUF) at Visakh Refinery, 
incorporating the world’s first and largest LC-MAX technology 
installation. For decades, the heavy residue at the bottom of 
the barrel was treated as the limit of what a refinery could 
achieve. As this asset advances through stabilisation towards 
its designed operating performance, this state-of-the-art 
facility will transform an unprecedented 93% of bottom-of-the-
barrel residue, thereby improving product value realisation. It 
has positioned Visakh Refinery as one of the most sophisticated 
refining complexes in the region. It is an asset that reflects 
not only engineering excellence but also HPCL’s confidence in 
investing for the future. The RUF is equipped with DigiSuite, 
which provides real-time process insights and monitors catalyst 
performance and equipment health through advanced data 
analytics.
At Mumbai Refinery, multiple optimisation initiatives contributed 
to improved reliability, higher throughput and enhanced 
profitability. During the year, Mumbai Refinery achieved its 
highest crude throughput of 10 MMT and recorded its lowest-
ever Fuel & Loss of 6.75 wt%.
Advanced Process Control (APC) was commissioned in all units 
of Visakh Refinery Modernisation Project (VRMP). Additionally, 
advanced digital process optimisation techniques including Real 
Time Optimiser (RTO) were commissioned across multiple units 
of Mumbai Refinery (MR) and Visakh Refinery (VR). These key 
digital initiatives will enhance operational efficiency, optimise 
energy utilisation and improve refinery performance.
Our continued investments in technology, d

igitisation and 
process optimisation will ensure that HPCL’s refining assets 
remain globally competitive and future-ready.
Strengthening Energy Infrastructure
HPCL continues to invest in strategic infrastructure that 
enhances capacity, strengthens supply chains and supports 
future growth.

Advancing the Energy Transition
The global transition towards cleaner energy presents both 
op

portunities and responsibilities. I am often asked how an 
oil company should think about a cleaner future. My answer 
is simple: not as a threat to be managed, but as a chance to 
be earned. India is already ahead of its global commitments—
and we intend to be among the builders of that future, not 
bystanders to it. At HPCL, we recognise that India’s transition 
pathway must balance the energy security, affordability and 
sustainability.
Accordingly, we are pursuing a diversified approach that 
combines conventional energy leadership with investments in 
emerging energy solutions.
During the year, renewable energy capacity increased to 241 
MW, advancing our pipeline of solar and wind assets. Green 
hydrogen remains a key strategic focus area. During FY 2025–26, 
Green H2 Purchase Agreement (GHPA) was signed with OCIOR 
Green Fuels Pvt Ltd for supply of 5 KTPA to Visakh Refinery 
on a BOO basis. Some of the year’s most quietly remarkable 
work happened at the edges of what we believed is possible: 
at Visakh, we turned used cooking oil—the very kind discarded 
from household kitchens—into sustainable aviation fuel; and in 
our laboratories, we coaxed bio-crude from seaweed. Modest 
steps today, perhaps, but they are the seeds of the energy 
company we are determined to become.
To contribute to India’s energy self-reliance, we achieved 
19.94% ethanol blending rate this year. Additionally, under the 
Government of India’s SATAT initiative to promote Compressed 
Biogas (CBG) as an alternative transport fuel, HPCL added three 
new CBG plants and increased the total CBG Plants under the 
SATAT scheme to 18. These efforts underscore our commitment 
to building a future-ready energy portfolio.

Sustainability continues to guide our strategic decisions and 
operational priorities.
During FY 2025–26, HPCL refineries achieved energy savings of 
86,542 SRFT and reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 0.28 
MTCO2e.
HPCL’s focus areas to advance its sus

tainable development 
agenda include decarbonisation, transition to clean energy, 
improved resource efficiency and responsible governance.
HPCL remains committed to achieving Net Zero emissions by 
2040 and continues to invest in initiatives that support this 
long-term ambition.
People: The Foundation of Our Success
We believe our success is largely fuelled by the dedication 
and commitment of our people. During FY 2025–26, employees 
completed over 74,268 person-days of training through various

capability-building programmes. Leadership development, 
digital upskilling and technical training remained key focus 
areas. We are dedicated to creating a safe, inclusive and 
empowering workplace where employees can thrive and 
contribute meaningfully.
Safety remains our highest priority, with over 11,752 safety 
training person-days delivered through immersive AR/VR 
modules to reinforce safety competencies.
We also launched SAFE 100, a 100-day organisation-wide safety 
drive to accelerate cultural change and reinforce operational 
discipline.
These initiatives reflect our unwavering focus on upskilling, 
safety and operational integrity.
Creating Shared Value
Our commitment to Nation-building extends beyond business 
operations. With CSR initiatives focused on education, 
healthcare, sanitation, women empowerment and skill 
development, we are laying the foundation for meaningful 
and lasting impact on communities. During FY 2025–26, HPCL 
allocated ₹97.05 crore towards CSR initiatives supporting around 
130 activities and projects for local area development in the 
vicinity of its operating locations. One of these stays with me 
above the rest. Under ‘Dil without Bill’, we helped fund heart 
surgeries for children from families who could never have 
afforded them. When you realise that a child is breathing 
easier tonight because of work this Corporation chose to do, 
you understand that nation-building is not merely a phrase in

port—it is the purpose that defines our existence.
Looking Ahead
The future presents immense opportunities for HPCL. India’s 
appetite for energy will only grow in the years ahead, and 
with it both our opportunity and our obligation. But I do not 
measure our future merely in barrels or volumes. I measure it 
in our readiness to change while staying true to who we are—a 
Company that keeps the Nation moving, lights its homes and 
working towards a cleaner horizon. The energy landscape will 
be reshaped by technology and by the demands of sustainability 
and your Company intends to help shape it rather than be 
shaped by it.
HPCL is well-positioned to thrive in this environment. Backed 
by strong fundamentals, strategic investments, world-class 
assets, a talented workforce and committed partners, we 
remain confident in our ability to create sustainable value 
while contributing meaningfully to India’s growth journey. Our 
greatest strength is the shared belief, held at every level of this

priorities and monitors performance across key environmental, 
social and governance (ESG) focus areas.

facilitating the preparation of statutory and voluntary 
sustainability disclosures.

and cross-functional approach involving:
• Committee of Functional Directors (CFD), providing strategic 
direction

and performance

effective execution, data governance, monitoring and

the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) for Central Public 
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). As the nodal authority for CPSEs, the 
DPE prescribes policies relating to remuneration, performance 
evaluation, organisational autonomy, financial delegation and 
human resource management, thereby ensuring consistency, 
transparency and accountability across public sector enterprises.
In accordance with these guidelines, HPCL has established a 
structured remuneration framework comprising pay scales, 
allowances, performance-related pay, retirement benefits and 
other applicable compensation components for Board-level 
executives and senior management. The remuneration policy 
and any revisions thereto are considered and approved by the 
Board of Directors and, wherever required, are submitted to the 
Administrative Ministry for issuance of Presidential Directives.

gover

with HPCL’s strategic objectives, promotes responsible business

MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT 
Materiality assessment forms the foundation of HPCL’s sustainability strategy by identifying and prioritising 
the environmental, social and governance (ESG) topics that have the greatest influence on long-term value 
creation, business performance and stakeholder decision-making. It supports effective risk management, strategic 
planning and transparent sustainability reporting.
Setting ESG Priorities for Long-term Value 
During FY 2025–26, HPCL reviewed its material ESG topics, 
building on the previous assessment to ensure continued 
alignment with evolving business priorities, stakeholder 
expectations and global sustainability practices. The review 
included validation of the existing materiality matrix against 
internationally recognised frameworks, including GRI 11 – Oil 
& Gas, SASB and IPIECA, together with benchmarking against 
industry peers and consideration of emerging regulatory 
developments, policy priorities and investor expectations.
Stakeholder perspectives were reaffirmed through 
structured engagement with employees (management 
and non-management), dealers, distributors, suppliers, 
contractors, transporters, customers, local communities, 
vulnerable and marginalised groups, and industry peers, 
ensuring that the assessment continued to reflect the 
expectations of key stakeholder groups.
Based on the review, the materiality matrix remained 
unchanged during FY 2025–26, reaffirming the relevance of 
HPCL’s existing sustainability priorities and their continued 
alignment with the Com

pany’s long-term strategy. To further 
strengthen ESG performance management, HPCL mapped 
defined Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to each material 
topic, enabling more effective monitoring, performance 
evaluation and integration of sustainability considerations 
into business planning and decision-making across the 
value chain.

highway network. The programme aims to establish

promoting safer highways, improved driver well-being 
and enhanced logistics efficiency.

hway transportation. Key facilities include:

ough the HP

hydrogen, battery technologies, renewable energy, carbon

diversify its business portfolio and strengthen its long term 
technological leadership.

Climate change is a strategic business priority for HPCL and 
is integrated into the Company’s long-term business strategy, 
enterprise risk management framework and investment 
decisions. Recognising the evolving physical and transition risks 
associated with climate change, HPCL continues to strengthen 
its climate resilience while pursuing opportunities arising from 
the transition to a low-carbon economy.
Aligned with its Net Zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2040 
ambition, the Company is embedding climate considerations 
across its refining, marketing, logistics, infrastructure 
development and corporate governance processes. HPCL’s 
decarbonisation strategy is driven by initiatives in renewable 
energy, energy efficiency, cleaner fuels, green hydrogen, 
biofuels, carbon management, circular economy practices and 
other low-carbon technologies.
Consistent with the principles of IFRS S2 Climate-related 
Disclosures, HPCL continues to enhance its climate governance, 
climate risk and opportunity assessment, greenhouse gas 
emissions management, scenario analysis and climate-
related performance monitoring. Through these initiatives, the 
Company aims to strengthen business resilience, support India’s 
energy transition and create sustainable long-term value for its 
stakeholders.
Governance
HPCL has established a robust governance framework to 
oversee its sustainability and climate transition agenda, 
ensuring effective Board oversight, executive accountability 
and integration of climate-related considerations into strategic 
decision-making. The Corporate Social Responsibility and 
Sustainable Development (CSR & SD) Committee of the Board, 
comprising Whole-time and Independent Directors and chaired 
by an Independent Director, provides strategic guidance on 
sustainability and climate-related matters. The Committee 
periodically reviews the Company’s progress towards its Net

Recognising the evolving energy landscape, HPCL continuously 
evaluates both transition risks arising from the shift towards 
a low-carbon economy and physical risks associated with 
climate change. The Company periodically reviews these risks 
and implements appropriate mitigation measures to safeguard 
its operations, assets and stakeholders.
Key Climate-related Risks
Transition Risks

solutions may progressively influence long-term demand

expectations may impact business operations, investments

events, rising temperatures and water stress may affect 
operational continuity, infrast

ructure resilience and supply 
chain reliability at certain locations.

infrastructure, EV charging and battery swapping networks

by 2040, supported by dedicated investments towards green 
and low-carbon business initiatives. 
•  Integrating energy efficiency measures across existing 
operations and upcoming projects, while establishing green 
hydrogen facilities at refinery locations. 
•  Strengthening research and innovation efforts focused on 
emerging green technologies, sustainable fuels and carbon 
management solutions.

Nine Locations Achieve Net Zero Operational Carbon Certification
India’s Net Zero ambition for 2070 gives HPCL its horizon; 
the Corporation’s own roadmap to Net Zero for Scope 1 and 
Scope 2 operational carbon by 2040 sets the pace. In FY 2025 
26, the Supply, Operations and Distribution(SOD) SBU turned 
that pledge into a national first.
Through sustained decarbonisation measures and sustainable 
operating practices, SOD SBU achieved Net Zero Operational 
Carbon Certification at nine locations, making HPCL the first 
company in India to certify a Net Zero Operational Facility. 
The milestone was celebrated at the 14th GreenCo Summit 
2025 in Hyderabad, held on the theme “Green Makes Business 
Sense” with the co theme “Beyond Commitments: Scaling 
Net Zero Action for 2030 and Beyond,” in the presence of Shri 
Duddilla Sridhar Babu, Honourable Minister for Information 
Technology, Electronics, Communications, Industries and 
Commerce, Government of Telangana, along with senior 
officials from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).
HPCL’s Secunderabad Terminal was honoured as India’s first 
location certified as a Net Zero Operational Carbon Location, 
followed by eight more: Miraj IRD, Kolkata Terminal, Sholapur 
IRD, Durgapur IRD, Visakh New White Oil Terminal, Haldia 
Terminal, Ramagundam IRD and Manmad IRD. Reinforcing this 
leadership, 12 SOD locations were awarded GreenCo Platinum 
and Gold Certification for their progress on sustainability.
The recognitio

n was hard earned. The Net Zero certification, 
conducted by CII, followed a rigorous evaluation: a 12 month 
data review, comprehensive physical inspections, and 
assessment across policy and commitment, GHG emission 
inventory, action plans, mitigation strategies, sustenance 
measures and Scope 3 screening. By meeting the standard 
for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, SOD SBU has set a new 
industry benchmark and given HPCL’s 2040 commitment a 
proven, replicable template.

Water Conservation Initiatives
Effluent Treatment and Recycling
HPCL adopts a circular approach to water management by 
maximising the treatment, recycling and reuse of wastewater 
across its operations. The Company has established Effluent 
Treatment Plants (ETPs) and Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) at 
major operational locations to ensure responsible wastewater 
management, minimise freshwater withdrawal and enhance 
water-use efficiency.
At refinery locations, wastewater is treated through physical, 
chemical, biological and tertiary treatment processes to meet 
the prescribed Minimum National Standards (MINAS) before 
being reused for operational purposes such as cooling tower 
make-up, fire water systems, utility services and horticulture. 
Effluent discharges are continuously monitored to ensure 
compliance with applicable environmental regulations and to 
maintain high standards of environmental performance.
During FY 2025–26, HPCL’s refineries and marketing locations 
recycled over 66,833 million kilolitres (KL) of water(including 
Bearing Cooling Water Recirculation), reinforcing the Company’s 
commitment to sustainable water stewardship and resource 
conservation.
Rainwater Harvesting
HPCL continues to strengthen water security through the 
implementation of rainwater harvesting systems across its 
operational locations. These initiatives support groundwater 
recharge, augment local water availability and reduce 
dependence on freshwater sources, particularly in water-
stressed regions.
Water Positivity 
HPCL is committed to strengthening its water stewardship 
practices by progressively transitioning towards water-positive 
operations. Recognising water as a critical natural capital 
resource, the Company aims to minimise freshwater withdrawal, 
maximise water recycling and reuse, and replenish water 
resour

ces through conservation and recharge initiatives across 
its operational footprint.
The Company’s water positivity strategy is built on four 
key pillars:
• Optimising freshwater consumption through process 
improvements, digital monitoring and water-efficient 
technologies.
• Maximising wastewater recycling and reuse by enhancing 
the performance and capacity of Effluent Treatment Plants 
(ETPs) and Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs).
• Replenishing water resources through rainwater harvesting, 
groundwater recharge, watershed development and 
community water conservation projects, particularly in 
water-stressed regions.
• Strengthening water governance through risk assessment, 
water accounting, performance monitoring and stakeholder 
engagement.

14.	 Dematerialisation of Shares:
As per Regulations 39 and 40 of the SEBI LODR, 2015, listed 
companies can process shareholders requests such as 
issuance of duplicate securities certificate, endorsement, 
sub- division/split, consolidation of securities certificate, 
transfer, transmission and transposition only in 
Dematerialised form with effect from January 25, 2022.
SEBI also vide its circular dated November 03, 2021, read 
with clarification dated December 14, 2021 has made it 
mandatory for all the shareholders to update the KYC 
details such as PAN, Address with pin code, Email Address, 
Mobile number, Bank Account details, Specimen Signature 
and advised RTA to process other service requests only 
after completion of updation of aforesaid details.
In view of the above, Shareholders holding shares in 
Physical form are required to approach RTA and follow the 
procedure indicated under Sr.No.13- Mandatory updation 
of KYC including PAN and Bank details as stated above.
Once the KYC details are updated and

procedure for 
duplicate, transmission, etc. is completed, RTA will issue 
a Letter providing the relevant details. Shareholders 
upon receipt of this Letter will have to submit the same 
along with other supporting documents to the RTA. After 
receipt of the original documents, RTA shall generate 
Demat Request Number (DRN) and share a web-link to the 
shareholders for confirmation on their registered mobile 
number and/or Email ID. Shareholders shall confirm the 
DRN via OTP within the stipulated time, failing which the 
demat request shall fail.
However, Members who are in possession of the 
original Share Certificates are requested to approach 
their respective Depository Participant (DP) for 
dematerialisation of shares.

8. Approval of Material Related Party 
Transactions with HPCL-Mittal Energy 
Limited
HPCL-Mittal Energy Limited (“HMEL”) is a Related Party 
as defined under Section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013 
(“Act”) read with Regulation 2 (1) (zb) of the SEBI (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015 (“SEBI LODR, 2015”).
The Company is proposing to enter into certain business 
transactions with HMEL during Financial Year 2027-28. The 
nature of transactions include purchase/sale of goods 
(such as, Petroleum/Petrochemical products, Crude etc.), 
availment/providing of services, lease rental etc. from/
to HMEL, and receipt of dividend. All transactions to 
be entered into by the Company with HMEL are in the 
ordinary course of business and are at arm’s length basis 
and necessary approvals as required in compliance of the 
provisions under the Act/ SEBI LODR, 2015 were obtained 
from the Audit Committee/Board.
It may be noted that as per the explanation to Regulation 
23 (1) of SEBI LODR, 2015, a transaction with a related 
party shall be considered material if the transaction(s) 
to be entered into individually or taken together with 
previous transactions during a Financial Year, exceeds 
₹3,000 Crore plus 2.5% of the annual consolidated 
turnover of the listed entity above ₹40,000 Crore or ₹5,000 
Crore, whichever is lower. Further, all Material Related 
Party Transactions require prior approval of the Members 
through a Resolution and no related party shall vote to 
approve such resolution whether an

entity is a related 
party to the particular transaction or not.
The transactions with HMEL for Financial Year 2027-28 
are estimated to be ₹ 1,46,000 Crore (Rupees One Lakh 
Forty Six Thousand Crore Only) and this amount exceeds 
above-mentioned threshold limit and therefore it is a 
Material Related Party Transaction. Accordingly, it requires 
prior approval of the Company by way of passing of an 
Ordinary Resolution.
Approval of the Members of the Company is therefore 
required in terms of Regulation 23 of the SEBI LODR, 2015 
by way of passing of an Ordinary Resolution for approval 
to the aforesaid Material Related Party Transactions to be 
entered for Financial Year 2027-28.
The Members at the 73rd AGM held on August 22, 2025, had 
granted approval for entering into Material Related Party 
Transactions with HMEL for up to ₹91,000 Crore during 
FY 2026-27. As a matter of abundant caution, the approval 
of the Members is sought for continuation of the said 
Material Related Party Transactions from the conclusion 
of the 74th AGM i.e. from August 26, 2026 till March 31, 2027, 
in line with the amendments to Regulation 23(4) of SEBI 
LODR, 2015, effective December 19, 2025.
Relevant documents, if any, in respect of the said item are 
available in electronic form for inspection by the Members 
of the Company upto the date of AGM.

holding shares of the Company may be deemed to be 
concerned or otherwise interested in the said Ordinary 
Resolution only to the extent of their shareholding.

for approval by the Members.

DEAR MEMBERS,
On behalf of the Board of Directors, it gives me immense pleasure in presenting this Report on the performance of your Corporation

Financial Year 2025 - 26 has been a year of strong operational and marketing performance with stellar profitability of ₹ 17,175

Refinery Performance
The financial year 2025–26 stands as a landmark year for HPCL 
Refineries, marked by exceptional operational and physical 
performance. Driven by a combination of proactive planning, 
technology-enabled optimization and agile decision-making, 
your Corporation achieved its highest-ever crude throughput 
of 26.04 MMT, surpassing the previous record of 25.27 MMT 
achieved in financial year 2024–25. This achievement was 
further reinforced by robust crude planning and agile supply 
chain management during the geopolitical disruptions in 
March 2026, enabling seamless operations and maximization 
of refinery throughput.
The Visakh Refinery delivered an outstanding performance 
by processing its highest-ever annual crude throughput of 
16.04 MMT (107% capacity utilization), supported by enhanced 
reliability and effective utilization of upgraded process units.

The Mumbai Refinery also demonstrated strong operational 
excellence, achieving a highest ever annual crude throughput 
of 10.00 MMT (105% capacity utilization), with sustained focus 
on efficiency, reliability, and optimization.
Strong operational performance and optimization initiatives 
led to record production of MS, HSD, LPG alongside achieving 
the distillate yield of 75.8 wt% during the year. Visakh Refinery 
achieved highest ever ATF production of 252 TMT. Mumbai 
Refinery also achieved its lowest ever Fuel & Loss of 6.75 wt% 
during the year.
The Refineries ability to adapt became exceptionally strong as 
we embraced new opportunity crudes and processed 10 new 
grades of crude for the first time. This surpassed the 8 numbers 
of new crude grades processed during financial year 2024-25. 
Further during the financial year 2025-26, 10 new grades were 
added to the Company’s crude basket, which now includes 188 
grades from various regions such as West Africa, Middle East, 
North America, South America, Mediterranean, North Sea, Far 
East, Russia and India.
India’s energy demand is set to grow, driven by its rapid economic 
growth. The rising demand for road transport fuels further adds 
to this increasing trend. Part of this increased demand is met 
by modernization and expansion of our refineries.
Your Corporation has successfully commissioned the Residue 
Upgradation Facility (RUF) at its Visakh Refinery during 
December 2025, featuring the world’s first and largest LC-Max 
unit—a major leap in advanced refining. With a capacity of 3.55 
MMTPA, this LC-Max–based RUF is among the world’s most 
advanced facilities, enabling 93% conversion of bottom-of-the-
barrel residues into high-value distillates. The unit enhances 
the refinery’s ability to process heavier and opportunity 
crudes while improving product quality and overall operational 
efficiency. RUF was provided with “DigiSuite” to have real time 
process insights, catalyst and critical equipment conditi

on 
using data analytics.
Lube Modernization & Bottom Upgradation Project is being 
taken up in Mumbai Refinery to increase the LOBS Production 
from current 475 KTPA to 764 KTPA and increase in Bitumen 
Production by approx. 487 KTPA, is progressing at good pace 
and has achieved significant milestones during the year.

Marketing Performance
In financial year 2025-26, your Corporation achieved its highest-
ever sales volume of 51.45 MMT (including refinery exports), 
registering a robust growth of 3.3% over the previous year. 
Retail, LPG, Aviation and Natural Gas Strategic Business Units 
(SBUs) achieved their highest-ever sales in the current financial 
year. Your Corporation remains steadfast in its commitment 
to meeting the evolving needs of customers and markets by 
ensuring a reliable and efficient supply of petroleum products 
through its extensive distribution network. The performance 
across various market business segments is summarized below:
In the Retail segment, your Corporation achieved its highest-
ever sales volume of 30.83 MMT and crossed the landmark 
milestone of 10 MMT in MS sales, recording an all-time high 
of 10.35 MMT. This achievement reflects sustained efforts to 
expand the retail footprint and enhance the customer value 
proposition through new services and green energy initiatives.
During the financial year, your Corporation commissioned 1,353 
new retail outlets, taking the total network to 25,098 outlets. 
Alternative fuels infrastructure also expanded significantly, 
with 215 new CNG stations added (total 2,253) and 285 additional 
EV charging facilities including battery swapping, taking the 
total number of EV enabled outlets to 5,533 at the year end, 
creating a charging ecosystem that delivers great convenience 
and range confidence for EV users, thereby accelerating the 
adoption of sustainable mobility.
Customer experience was enhance

d through ITPS (Integrated 
Transaction Processing System)-enabled accurate billing, faster 
service delivery, and strict adherence to SOPs supported by 
CCTV-based monitoring. The Corporation’s flagship loyalty 
program, DriveTrack Plus, continued to gain traction in the 
commercial vehicle segment Your Corporation continued to 
strengthen its digital customer experience through the HP 
Pay app, a state-of-the-art digital payment platform offering 
seamless, secure, and contactless fuel transactions. With 
advanced voice-enabled payment solutions, the app further 
enhances convenience by enabling customers to initiate and 
complete fuel payments effortlessly at HPCL retail outlets.
Highway presence was further strengthened through the 
Wayside Amenities (WSAs) initiative, with 14 new WSAs and 
Direct Dealerships commissioned, taking the total to 53. 
Additionally, 124 Apna Ghar trucker facilities were established, 
enhancing the comfort and convenience of the driver community 
by providing safe parking, clean washrooms, cooking facilities, 
and resting areas to help reduce driver fatigue and promote 
safer journeys.
Under the Non-Fuel Business (NFB) vertical, your Corporation 
expanded partnerships with well-known national and 
international QSR brands to increase its footprint at retail 
outlets. New tie-ups were entered into with Domino’s Pizza, 
Food On Wheel, Nirula’s, Nescafe, Desire Foods, HungerBox 
and FoodMojo for QSR and dhaba expansion with a focus on 
enhancing customer offerings at retail outlets.
As part of the Corporation’s environmental commitment, bulk 
Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) dispensing facilities were made 
available at select outlets, while packed DEF was available 
across the retail outlet network.
Sustainability initiatives were further scaled up, with solar 
panels installed at an additional 1,471 retail outlets. At the 
year end, a total of 23,824 outlets (~95% of the network) were 
solarized with installed capacity of 93.88 MW.

major capital expenditure cycle nearing completion, including 
key projects such as the Visakh Refinery Residue Upgradation

residual long-term funding requirements being met through

facilities from banks.

Risk Management Policy
We operate in a dynamic environment which not only provides 
opportunities but also exposes the business to various 
internal and external risks. Your Corporation recognizes that 
all facets of its business involve significant risks and that 
its actions are increasingly exposed to greater scrutiny by 
the public, regulators, investors, and other stakeholders. To 
proactively identify and manage key risks for achieving our 
strategic objectives and enable the Corporation to deal with 
these enhanced business challenges and risks, an effective 
and pragmatic risk management framework has been 
institutionalized across the organization.
Your Corporation has fortified its Enterprise Risk Management 
(ERM) framework by incorporating the best practices 
recommended by internationally recognized standards such 
as COSO ERM 2

017 and ISO 31000:2018. Our ERM Policy is 
periodically reviewed and encompasses a comprehensive array 
of risks that could impact our strategic objectives and overall 
performance. The objective is to integrate risk identification 
and management in the day-to-day operations of the business, 
wherein risk is continuously identified, assessed, monitored, 
graded and managed to an acceptable level. Your Corporation 
has engaged reputed external consultant to provide additional 
perspective and support the ERM processes.
A systematic process of periodic risk reviews is in place across 
all key Strategic Business Units (SBUs) and Functions. The Risk 
Management Committee meets periodically, at least twice 
in a financial year, to ensure that appropriate methodology, 
systems and processes are in place to review these risks as 
well as monitor the progress of implementation of various 
mitigation measures. The Board is also updated regularly on 
the risk review and mitigation measures of the identified risk.

Procurement Of Goods & Services From 
MSEs
The Government of India has notified a Public Procurement 
Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) Order, 2012, and its 
amendments thereto. In line with said policy, your Corporation 
has set an annual goal of sourcing a minimum procurement of 
25% of its total requirements from MSEs, and within it, 4% of 
the total requirement has been earmarked for procurement 
from MSEs owned by SC/ST entrepreneurs and another 3% 
from women entrepreneurs. For the benefit of MSEs, the MSE 
procurement details are regularly uploaded on the Sambandh 
Portal of the Ministry of MSME, besides displaying the Annual 
Procurement Plan on the Corporation’s website.
The centralized procurement department of your corporation is 
ISO 9001:2015 Certified & also conform to ISO 20400:2017. Your 
organization also prioritizes the implementation of government 
policies aimed at strengthening the MSME ecosystem and 
promoting indigenization, developmental orders, and start-
up orders.
Against the set target of 25% of the total procurement for 
financial year 2025-26, your Corporation has achieved 59.42% 
(₹ 6,679 Crore) of procurement of goods and services from MSEs, 
excluding items that are beyond the scope of MSEs. Also, your 
Corporation has also surpassed the procurement from MSE SC/
ST & MSE Women by Achieving 5.10% (₹ 573 Crore) from MSE SC/
ST and 4.30% (₹ 484 Crore) from MSE Women against the target 
of 4% & 3% respectively. The excluded items are crude oil, 
petroleum products, logistics costs through shipping, railways 
and pipelines, LNG/Natural Gas, API line pipes, OEM spares, OEM 
services, proprietary items and services, technology licenses 
and licensor-mandated items, and plants and machinery (single 
item value equal to or more than ₹ 100 Crore).
To promote the objectives of procurement

from MSEs as 
laid down in Public Procurement Policy, Organized 25 vendor 
meets in collaboration with National SC/ST Hub (NSSH), 
attended by 426 vendors, focused on promoting MSE SC/ST 
vendor onboarding, Participation in 8 numbers of National 
Vendor Development Programs (NVDP) arranged by MoMSME 
and 103 nos of Inhouse Vendor meets were organized by CPO 
for training the vendor on procurement process, resolving of 
issues and guiding them on policies. During these meetings, 
the Corporation procurement processes were articulated 
through detailed presentations to MSE vendors with the intent 
of increasing awareness on vendor registration processes, 
tendering processes, the TReDS platform, procurement on the 
GeM platform, etc. The implementation of various government 
directives/policies for providing relief to MSMEs and promoting 
the indigenization of products and services was also explained 
during the programme.
Your Corporation is registered with the TReDS Digital platform, 
an institutional mechanism set up by the Reserve Bank of India 
to facilitate the trade receivable financing of Micro Small and 
Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) from corporate buyers through 
multiple financiers. Integrating its ERP system with Five of 
the service providers, namely A.Treds Ltd., Mynd Solutions Pvt. 
Ltd., Receivables Exchange of India Ltd. C2 TReDS platform and 
DTX (KredX Platform Pvt Limited, the Corporation has enabled 
MSMEs to auction their trade receivables at competitive rates 
through online bidding by financiers. Numerous MSME vendors 
have onboarded this platform and benefited from the bill 
discounting facility that provides liquidity.

Research and Development
Hindustan Petroleum Green Research & Development Centre 
(HPGRDC) was set up with the objective of developing solutions 
for existing and new business areas. Today, HPGRDC stands not 
just as an R&D Centre for the Refineries but as a beacon of 
excellence across the diverse spectrum of our industry. From 
Refining to Marketing, from Lubes to LPG, and from energy 
transition initiatives to ground-breaking technologies, its 
footprint spans far and wide, leaving an enduring legacy of 
innovation and creativity.
In the pursuit of excellence, during financial year 2025-26, 
HPGRDC signed 8 MoUs for collaborative innovation and 
business development with various national and international 
organizations/institutes during the year. These collaborations, 
undertaken with the clear objective of becoming solution 
providers, signify our commitment to fostering synergistic 
relationships and value creation across the industry.
In addition to our collaborative endeavours and technological 
advancements, we achieved a significant patent milestone of 
779 patent filings and received 312 patent grants. In financial 
yea

r 2025-26, HPGRDC filed 118 patents, taking the cumulative

cumulative patents granted to 312. This solidifies HPGRDC 
position as one of the fastest growing research institute in 
intellectual property creation and innovation.
HPCL remains steadfast in its commitment to indigenization, 
harnessing homegrown talent and expertise to develop 
technologies and products with significant impact. Last year, 
our focus on indigenous solutions led to the development 
of ground-breaking technologies and products that not only 
showcased our technical prowess but also made substantial 
contributions to our operations and the industry at large.
HPGRDC continued innovation with the objective of developing 
solutions for existing and new business areas, with the special 
focus on green chemistry principles. HPGRDC successfully 
developed and 18 Nos. new products catering to refinery 
solutions, corrosion solutions, lube formulations etc. were

HPCL’s commitment to innovation led to scale-up of R&D 
developed catalysts to commercial scale for utilization in 
refineries. Some of which include HGU PDS Catalyst, HP 
DAK Catalyst (Catalyst for DAK technology), HP DHT (Diesel 
Hydrotreating) catalyst, HP NHT (Naphtha Hydrotreating) 
catalyst, HP AMT (Advanced Matrix Technology FCC catalyst).
Global Technology Centre (GTC) of HPGRDC has undertaken 
various innovative initiatives to improve processes, increase 
operational efficiencies and reduce energy consumption of 
HPCL Refineries. Technical solutions were provided on issues 
such as increasing feed rate in VR HGU PDS, resolving NSU 
pressure drop fluctuation issue, processing off-spec (colour)

green hydrogen initiatives, HPGRDC is working on development 
of advanced Alkaline-AEM electrolyser technology through 
an integrated approach combining electrode materials 
development, stack engineering and system optimization. 
Currently, this is being scaled up to 1 MW scale. The salient 
features include higher hydrogen purity from AEM stack, low 
severity operation and comparatively less power consumption.
Furthermore, HPCL has made significant strides in battery 
technology development, exemplified by our in-house 
innovations in lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. The 
lithium-ion cylindrical cell, featuring inhouse Lithium Nickel 
Manganese Oxide cathode and graphite anode, has achieved 
impressive energy density. Additionally, beyond Lithium-
ion initiatives, ground breaking work on development of 
cathode materials for Sodium ion batteries have resulted in 
successful development of high-voltage cathode materials, 
such as Sodium Vanadium Fluorophosphate and layered 
oxide cathode materials. These have culminated in the scale 
up of cathode material and demonstration of sodium-ion 
batteries, showcasing our commitment to diversifying energy 
storage solutions.

Corporate Governance Report
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (“Company/HPCL”) 
is a Government Company and a ‘Maharatna’ Central Public 
Sector Enterpris

e (“CPSE”) listed on BSE Limited (“BSE”) and 
National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”) and governed 
by SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI LODR, 2015”) and Guidelines on 
Corporate Governance (“DPE Guidelines”) issued by Department 
of Public Enterprises (“DPE”).
As required under Schedule V of SEBI LODR, 2015, disclosure 
relating to “Related Party” and “Management Discussion and 
Analysis” have been dealt with in other parts of this Integrated 
Annual Report while the Corporate Governance Report is 
appended below.
Philosophy on Corporate Governance
At HPCL, Corporate Governance is to meet the Stakeholders 
aspirations and Societal expectations. The key principles on 
which this edifice is built includes well developed internal 
controls, systems and processes, transparency in business 
operations, performance and financial position, clearly defined 
management performance & accountability and full adherence 
to compliances and disclosures.
This is made possible due to its well-defined Policy framework 
which includes Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior 
Management Personnel, Integrity Pact to enhance transparency 
in business operations, Public Grievance Redressal Mechanism, 
Whistleblower Policy, Empowerment and Authority Manual and 
the Procurement Manual.
Being a Government Company, its activities are reviewed by 
several external authorities like the Comptroller & Auditor 
General of India (“C&AG”), the Central Vigilance Commission 
(“CVC”), Parliamentary Committees etc. The Annual Report on 
the affairs and working of the Company along with comments of 
C&AG is also placed regularly in both the Houses of Parliament.
Structure of Corporate Governance in HPCL
At the apex level of the structure is the Board which has 
constituted several sub-committees viz. Audit Committee, 
Risk Management Committee, Nomination & Remuneration 
Committee, Stakeholders Relationship Committee, CSR and 
Sustainability Deve

lopment Committee and Project Evaluation 
and Review Committee, the composition of which and the 
meetings held during the Financial Year 2025-26 are separately

of transparency and better understanding to the public 
at large.

to coordinate, facilitate and oversee its implementation.

time period of 30 days through the Online RTI portal

Global Energy Scenario
Global energy demand growth slowed to 1.3% in CY 2025, 
down from 2.2% in CY 2024. A softer economic outlook, 
moderate growth of energy-intensive industries across some 
regions, reduced cooling demand and quicker efficiency gains 
contributed to the slowdown in demand growth.
Renewables: Solar PV, the largest single source of growth, met 
more than 25% of the incremental demand. This was the first 
time on record that a modern renewable source contributed 
the largest share of global energy demand. The 2025 increase 
in solar PV of 600 terawatt-hours (TWh) was the largest-
ever increase in electricity generation by any source in one 
year, outside periods of post-crisis recovery. Low-emission 
sources combined – solar, wind, nuclear, hydropower and 
other renewables – contributed nearly 60% of the growth in 
global demand.

Natural Gas: Gas demand growth decreased significantly in

of the year.
Coal: Demand for coal rose by 0.4% in CY 2025, slower than the 
1.4% rise in CY 2024, due to cooler weather and strong growth 
in renewables.
Oil: The demand for oil slowed to 0.7% in CY 2025, mainl

y due 
to weaker growth in petrochemical feedstocks, especially in 
China. Continued growth in electric vehicles also kept growth 
in oil demand for road transport muted.
Global electricity demand increased by 3% year-on-year in CY 
2025, slowing from 4.4% the year before. While demand from 
electric vehicles (+38%) and data centres (+17%) grew rapidly, 
they represented only small portions of the overall electricity 
demand increase. The main drivers of growth remained 
industry, household appliances and commercial buildings 
(excluding data centres).
Indian Energy Scenario
Energy Demand in India grew by 1.1% in CY 2025, which was 
among the lowest rates recorded in recent years. In CY 2025, 
electricity demand in India grew by 1.4% y-o-y, marking 
the weakest growth rate since at least 1972, excluding the 
decline seen in 2020 during the pandemic. The muted growth 
was largely driven by milder weather conditions, with fewer 
heatwaves in the summer and an early onset of the monsoon 
season, which eased cooling needs and reduced peak loads 
during the hottest months.
Oil demand growth in India sharply slowed to only 0.6% in 
CY 2025. The gap between the low growth rate and India’s 
rapid GDP expansion is mainly due to the significant increase 
in biofuel use in road transport, which grew by about 50% in 
2025. Additionally, a strong monsoon season reduced transport 
activity. The main driver of increased oil product demand was 
LPG, mainly for clean cooking. This trend is supported by 
government initiatives encouraging LPG use in households, 
particularly in rural regions.
India’s natural gas consumption decreased by 3.5% in CY 2025, 
with the demand for gas in power generation dropping nearly 
10% due to robust growth in renewables and milder weather.
Renewable electricity generation grew by 20% in CY 2025, 
the strongest annual increase in the last decade. Solar PV 
generation led the growth, up by 24% in 2025, a sharp rise from 
15% in CY 2024, which was booste

d by substantial cost declines. 
India’s annual renewable capacity additions increased by 
almost 60% in 2025, the fastest growth among major markets. 
This was driven by the commissioning of almost 50 GW of solar 
PV. India’s wind additions, while much smaller compared with 
solar PV, doubled in 2025 to reach over 6 GW.
The scale of the nation’s energy appetite was significant, 
with total petroleum product consumption reaching 243.2 
million metric tonnes (MMT), natural gas consumption at 68.5 
BCM and domestic crude oil processing at 272.1 MMT for the 
FY 2025–26 (PE).

Dated Brent crude oil prices opened FY 2025–26 at US$ 67.7 
per barrel in April 2025 and averaged US$ 70.3 per barrel over 
the year, with sharp volatility through the final quarter. For 
the first three quarters, prices trended lower as the market 
focused on a looming supply surplus and weaker demand 
expectations driven by escalating U.S.–China trade tariffs. 
Production discipline by the Organization of the Petroleum 
Exporting Countries and its allies (OPEC+) and geopolitical 
tensions in Eastern Europe provided intermittent support, but 
rising non-OPEC+ output, led by the United States and Brazil, 
capped prices. Sentiment shifted decisively in Q4. A military 
escalation in West Asia in March 2026 led to the closure of the 
Strait of Hormuz (through which approximately 20% of global 
oil trade transits), producing a supply shock that drove prices 
sharply higher and closed the year with extreme volatility.

averaging US$ 63.7 per barrel compared with US$ 69.1 per barrel

regional trade. This downward trend continued in November 
2025, with prices averaging US$ 63.7 per barrel, as optimism

geopolitical risk premium. By December 2025, prices softened 
further to US$ 62.7 per barrel, pressured by forecasts of a 
significant global oil surplus in early 2026. Additionally, the 
market saw increased supply as new intermediaries began 
handling Russian oil exports that were previously restricted. 
Overall, the quarter saw a shift from geopolitical concerns 
toward a bearish outlook driven by rising supply and trade-
related demand headwinds.
Dated Brent crude oil prices rose sharply during fourth quarter 
of FY 2025–26, averaging US$ 80.6 per barrel compared with 
US$ 63.7 per barrel in Q3. Prices remained relatively stable 
in January 2026 at US$ 66.8 per barrel and February 2026 at 
US$ 71.2 per barrel, as the market balanced a projected global 
supply surplus against persistent ‘war talk’ involving Iran. 
However, the market environment changed substantially in 
March 2026, with prices averaging US$ 103.9 per barrel. This 
surge was driven by an escalating military conflict between 
Iran, the U.S., and Israel, which led to the effective closure of 
the Strait of Hormuz. As this critical chokepoint handles nearly 
20% of the

supply shock, sending prices briefly toward the US$ 130 per 
barrel mark. The benchmark for Middle Eastern high sulphur 
crude oil, Dubai crude oil price, even touched high of US$ 169 
per barrel. This geopolitical crisis overshadowed fundamental 
surplus concerns, ending the financial year with extreme 
price volatility.

the primary driver that sustained Singapore refining profitability through the supply shock.
Domestic Petroleum Products Consumption 
India’s petroleum product consumption sustained its upward momentum in FY 2025–26, increasing by 1.7% to 243.2 MMT from 
239.2 MMT in the previous year. The demand landscape during the year was shaped by robust industrial activity, expanding 
infrastructure and a surge in the aviation sector. The fiscal year was also marked by significant price fluctuations in the Indian 
Basket of Crude, which saw a sharp increase in early 2026 due to geopolitical tensions in West Asia.

The primary drivers of

growth were the three key petroleum products — Petrol (MS), Diesel (HSD) and LPG. MS consumption 
maintained its strong upward trajectory, reaching a new high of 42.6 MMT, registering an impressive 6.5% growth, supported by 
rising automobile sales and increased mobility. HSD, accounting for nearly 39% of total consumption, grew by 3.6% to 94.7 MMT, 
reflecting sustained momentum in infrastructure development, freight movement, and overall economic activity. LPG consumption 
also continued its steady growth, increasing by 6% to 33.2 MMT, driven by household and industrial demand; however, growth in 
the latter half of the year faced competition from the expanding Piped Natural Gas (PNG) network in urban areas. 
Despite multiple headwinds faced by the aviation sector during the year, ATF consumption recorded a moderate growth of 2%, 
indicating resilience in air travel demand. Bitumen consumption rose by 3%, supported by continued focus on road construction 
and infrastructure development.
In contrast, the market also exhibited structural shifts. Naphtha consumption declined sharply by 9.9%, primarily due to substitution 
by natural gas and other alternative feedstocks. Similarly, Fuel Oil consumption registered a marginal decline of 1.5%, reflecting 
policy-driven transitions towards cleaner fuels and targeted restrictions on its usage.

Outlook
As CY 2026 progresses, the global economy is facing a shock 
stemming from a military conflict in West Asia that has persisted 
since late February 2026. The conflict has caused significant 
humanitarian suffering, damage to critical infrastructure and 
disruptions to maritime and air traffic in the region. Its effects 
are being transmitted globally

through higher commodity 
prices, rising inflation expectations, particularly in energy and 
food, and heightened risk aversion in financial markets. The 
global economic impact will depend on the duration, intensity 
and scope of the conflict, which remain uncertain.
Against this backdrop, the International Monetary Fund’s 
World Economic Outlook projects global GDP growth of 3.1% in 
CY 2026. Growth is expected to improve modestly to 3.2% in 
CY 2027, contingent on an easing of these global pressures.

Despite these headwinds, the underlying fundamentals of

and financial institutions, along with supportive monetary and

Factors driving global energy demand are shifting. Demographic 
influences are waning as population growth slows. The share 
of the cement, iron, and steel industries in global energy 
demand growth is declining, while the share of industries such 
as plastics and manufacturing is expanding. Space cooling 
is a key demand driver as temperatures rise, especially in 
emerging economies with rising incomes. Structural changes in 
economies and the emergence of new demand drivers, such as 
AI and clean-technology manufacturing, are driving up energy

consumption in specific industrial subsectors. Emerging sources 
of electricity demand, such as electric vehicles, heat pumps 
and highly concentrated loads like data centres, are expected 
to grow rapidly. Furthermore, total electricity generation from 
renewables is overtaking that from coal. Together, renewables 
and nuclear are expected to account for around half of global 
electricity generation by 2030.
India has already achieved 50% of its installed capacity from 
non-fossil fuel sources ahead of its 2030 target under the Paris 
Agreement. Between 2026 and 2030, the country is expected to 
add almost 300 GW of renewable power capacity.

C. STRATEGY
HPCL’s strategy takes a balanced and pragmatic approach 
to the evolving energy landscape. The Corporation 
continues to strengthen its core business in traditional 
fuels, ensuring security, affordability and supply reliability 
for India’s growing needs. In parallel, it is reducing the 
carbon intensity of refining operations through residue 
upgradation, fuel substitution (green hydrogen replacing 
grey hydrogen), electrification and renewable integration. 
The Corporation is also accelerating investments in 
emerging and alternate fuels, including biofuels, LNG, 
EV charging infrastructure and green hydrogen. During 
the year, as part of its green initiative, HPCL awarded 
a work order for a 5 KTA green hydrogen project at its 
Visakh Refinery.
This dual-track approach allows HPCL to meet today’s 
demand efficiently while positioning the Corporation as 
a leader in the energy transition, aligned to market shifts 
and the evolving expectations of customers, regulators 
and investors.
HPCL is also leveraging its R&D infrastructure at HP 
Green R&D Centre (HPGRDC) to develop products and 
technologies for

the energy transition.
The strategy rests on three pillars: strengthening existing 
refining and marketing businesses, building new growth 
engines in petrochemicals and natural gas and pursuing 
green and emerging opportunities, with technology and 
innovation as cross-cutting enablers.
The company has undertaken several large-scale projects 
to strengthen its existing businesses in refining and 
marketing. HPCL commissioned Residue Upgradation 
Facility (RUF) at Visakh Refinery, featuring the world’s first 
and largest LC-Max unit expanding refinery capacity by 3.55 
MMTPA. The LC-Max–based RUF is among the world’s most 
advanced facilities, enabling ~93% conversion of bottom-
of-the-barrel residues into high-value distillates. Beyond 
the  capacity expansion, the unit enhances the refinery’s 
ability to process heavier and opportunity crudes and lifts 
the Nelson Complexity Index to 11.6, maximising recovery 
of high-value products with minimal residue generation.
Progressive commissioning of the greenfield refinery-
cum-petrochemical complex through HPCL’s joint venture, 
HPCL Rajasthan Refineries Limited (HRRL), is underway. 
The HRRL project comprises 9 MMTPA of refining capacity, 
including 2.4 MMTPA of petrochemical capacity. Separately, 
the Corporation continued to strengthen its polymer 
brand HP Durapol during FY 2025–26 by marketing HDPE, 
LLDPE and PP grades in strategic markets.
Refinery expansion has been accompanied by build-out 
of the supply and distribution network to evacuate the 
increased output. These major projects will enhance 
HPCL’s capacity and will create value in the coming years.
The LNG import and regasification terminal of HPCL LNG 
Limited (HPLNG), a wholly owned subsidiary of HPCL, at 
Chhara Port in Gujarat is now operational. An MoU was 
signed with the Indian Gas Exchange (IGX) to list spare LNG 
storage capacity slots (both quantity- and period-based), 
enhancing commercial flexibility and secondary-market 
participation. This

is in addition to term LNG contracts 
secured for supply continuity for captive consumption. 
HPCL’s wholly owned subsidiary for green businesses, 
HP Renewable and Green Energy Limited (HPRGE), is 
operational and consolidating various opportunities. 
Two Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) plants have been set up

D. INTEGRATED MARGIN MANAGEMENT
The Integrated Margin Management (IMM) group 
enhances Net Corporate Realisation (NCR) by planning 
and optimising end-to-end supply chain logistics from 
crude oil to customers and aligning the strategic business 
units to a common corporate goal. During FY 2025–26, IMM 
continued to drive HPCL’s planning operations against 
this objective. 
IMM captured margin opportunities by optimising the 
processing slate across regular, new and opportunity crude 
grades available at competitive rates at both refineries. 
These efforts helped HPCL achieve its highest-ever crude 
throughput in FY 2025–26. Overall value realisation was 
enhanced by increased production, higher-value product 
sales and improved demand forecast accuracy.
The IMM group drives margin improvement ideas generated 
across the Corporation through an Idea Management 
Office (IMO), Idea Junction, which tracks execution. During 
FY 2025–26, 2,387 ideas were submitted and evaluated. To 
strengthen employee participation across all SBUs, the 
IMO organised idea workshops, and five SBUs launched 
theme-based idea campaigns.

judgments and there are no material changes.

judgments and estimates to determine the possible outcome of 
these disputes. The Company has disputes pending at various

No.- 53 and para (vii) (b) - Annexure I of this report).

key audit matter.

deliberations and estimates for possible outflow and opinion 
of internal experts of the Company in relation to such disputed 
tax positions.

AS 37 “Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets”.

Inventories
How the Key Audit matter was addressed
The verification and valuation of inventories, is a significant 
area that involves considerable management judgment in the 
application of accounting policies and estimation techniques. 
Since, these judgments have a significant impact on the amounts 
recognized in the Standalone Financial Statements, we have 
identified this area as a key audit matter. (Refer Note No. 11)

We evaluated the inventory monitoring and control system and 
noted that the physical verification of inventories is done by the 
Management at reasonable intervals.

Our audit teams conducted physical verification of inventories 
on a sample basis at various locations. However, since physical 
verification at every location is not possible, in such cases we 
placed reliance on the physical verification procedures carried 
out by the Management.

For inventories held at third-party locations, we relied on the 
Company’s system of re

cord-keeping related to such inventories.

We also tested, on a sample basis, the values used for 
determining net realisable value and cost of inventories, and 
verified their consistency with the inventory valuation records 
and related accounting entries.

We assessed that the valuation of inventories is in compliance 
Ind AS 2.

Leases (Ind AS 116)
How the Key Audit matter was addressed
The Company has adopted Ind AS 116 - Leases, which requires 
recognition of right-of-use assets and corresponding lease 
liabilities for all applicable lease arrangements. The application 
of this standard involves significant judgments, including 
determination of the lease term (considering renewal and 
termination options), identification of lease and non-lease 
components, and discounting of lease liabilities.
Given the materiality of lease balances and the significant 
management judgment involved in measurement and recognition, 
this area was considered as a key audit matter. (Refer Note No. 3 & 42)
•
Evaluating the Company’s process for identification of 
lease contracts.
•
Testing a sample of lease agreements to assess whether they 
meet the definition of a lease under Ind AS 116.
•
Assessing the reasonableness of key assumptions such as lease 
term and discount rate.
•
Verifying the mathematical accuracy of lease liability and 
right-of-use asset calculations.
•
Evaluating the adequacy of disclosures in the standalone 
financial statements.

Corporation Limited (the “Company”) and based on

1.	
Assess the fair valuation of all the investments, both 
quoted and unquoted, made directly by the Company 
or through Trusts, for Post retirement benefits of 
the employees. This includes verifying valuation 
methodologies, ensuring consistency with Ind AS 
and reviewing supporting documentation. The auditor 
shall provide a brief note on the valuation approach, 
its reasonability, and compliance with applicable

All the investments, made directly by the Co

mpany or 
through Trusts, for Post-retirement benefits of the 
employees have been valued appropriately in accordance 
with the applicable financial reporting framework and 
applicable regulations. The valuation approach and 
valuation methodologies applied by the Company for these 
investments is appropriate. Following is the brief note:
	
The Company has four post-employment plans managed 
through separate trusts. These plans are pertaining to 
Provident Fund (PF), Gratuity, Post-Retirement Medical 
Benefit (PRMB), and Superannuation benefit (SBFS).
	
Investments by PF Trust are as per Employees’ Provident 
Fund & Miscellaneous Provisions Act guidelines and 
include Government Securities, State Development Loans, 
Government-guaranteed bonds, corporate bonds, Mutual 
Funds (ETFs), InvITs, liquid funds etc., and investments 
by PRMB Trust are also of similar nature. Gratuity and 
SBFS trusts primarily invest in group insurance schemes 
with life insurance companies, including traditional and 
market-linked products.
	
The Valuation of investments has been carried-out 
by the registered valuer, for carrying-out necessary 
accounting as per Indian Accounting Standards. The 
valuer has applied the Market Approach for actively traded 
instruments using sources such as FBIL, FIMMDA, AMFI, 
and stock exchanges, and the Income Approach (DCF 
method using YTM) for illiquid instruments. The valuation 
approach adopted is reasonable and is in compliance 
with applicable regulations, and there are no material 
deviations or misstatements.

ANNEXURE III TO THE INDEPENDENT AUDITORS’ REPORT
(Referred to in paragraph 3(g) under “Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements” of our report of even date)
Report on the Internal Financial Controls with reference 
to Standalone Financial Statements under clause (i) of 
sub-section 3 of section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 
(“the Act”)
We have audited the internal financial controls with reference 
to standalone financial statements of Hindustan Petroleum 
Corporation Limited (“the Company”) as of March 31, 2026 
in conjunction with our audit of the standalone financial 
statements of the Company for the year ended on that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal 
Financial Controls
The Board of Directors of the Company is responsible for 
establishing and maintaining internal financial controls 
based on the internal control over financial reporting criteria 
established by the Company considering the essential 
components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note 
on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting 
(“the Guidance Note”) issued by the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India (the “ICAI”). These responsibilities include 
the design, implementation and maintenance of adequate 
internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial 
statements of the Company that were operating effectively 
for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct of its business, 
including adherence to company’s policies, the safeguarding of 
its assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, 
the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and 
the timely preparation of reliable financial info

rmation, as 
required under the Act.
Auditors’ Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company's 
internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial 
statements of the Company based on our audit. We conducted 
our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note issued by the 
ICAI and the Standards on Auditing prescribed under Section 
143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit of 
internal financial controls. Those Standards and the Guidance 
Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and 
plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance 
about whether adequate internal financial controls with 
reference to standalone financial statements were established 
and maintained and if such controls operated effectively in all 
material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit 
evidence about the adequacy of the internal financial controls 
with reference to standalone financial statements and their 
operating effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial controls 
with reference to standalone financial statements included 
obtaining an understanding of internal financial controls over 
financial reporting, assessing the risk that a material weakness 
exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating 
effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk. 
The procedures selected depend on the auditors’ judgement, 
including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement 
of the standalone financial statements, whether due to fraud 
or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained, is 
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion 
on the Company’s internal financial controls with reference to 
standalone financial statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls over 
Financial Reporting
A Company's internal financial control over financial reporting is 
a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding 
the rel

iability of financial reporting and the preparation of 
financial statements for external purposes in accordance with 
generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal 
financial control over financial reporting includes those policies 
and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records 
that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the 
transactions and dispositions of the assets of the Company; (2) 
provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded 
as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in 
accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and 
that receipts and expenditures of the Company are being made 
only in accordance with authorisations of management and 
directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance 
regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised 
acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company's assets that 
could have a material effect on the financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial 
Controls Over Financial Reporting
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial 
controls over financial reporting, including the possibility 
of collusion or improper management override of controls, 
material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and 
not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the 
internal financial controls over financial reporting to future 
periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial control 
over financial reporting may become inadequate because of 
changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with 
the policies or procedures may deteriorate.
